title: How To Handle Unplanned Interruptions
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles the stress of unplanned classroom interruptions — fire alarms, power outages, schedule changes, colleagues dropping the ball — arguing that a teacher's rising internal stress in these moments transfers directly to students and worsens their behavior. His proposed solution is maintaining deliberate 'professional distance' from the job and from situations outside one's control, paired with daily practice such as morning visualization, so that a teacher can view chaos from a broader vantage point rather than reacting emotionally in the moment. He frames this as a discipline that must be practiced daily until it becomes second nature, even for naturally anxious people, eventually producing a calm default state that lets a teacher think clearly and choose the right response quickly. The piece closes by reframing unexpected disruptions as minor and manageable once this distance is established, rather than something that derails an entire day.
points: A teacher's rising internal stress during an interruption transfers directly to students, worsening their behavior in the moment.
Cultivate deliberate 'professional distance' from students, the job, and situations outside your control to make clearer, less emotional decisions.
Morning visualization and daily practice of staying calm under stress can turn even a naturally anxious teacher into someone unshakeable in a crisis.
Maintaining this distance produces clearer thinking during chaos, letting you quickly choose the right path and get back on track without a hitch.
With practice, unexpected disruptions stop ruining the moment or the day — they become, in Linsin's words, 'a penny on the tracks, nothing more.'
quotes: Events and incidents out of your control invade your well-ordered peace like the hordes of Cimbri.
Your present mood and disposition also transfer to your students. The more anxious and frustrated you feel, the worse they’ll behave.
Well, here at SCM we’ve long promoted the benefits of maintaining a professional distance—from students, from the job, and from situations out of your control.
But it takes work. It takes daily practice. It takes discipline to work at it every day until it becomes second nature.
For those who practice the discipline of never getting too invested or deep in the emotive weeds, unexpected events act as a trigger to draw back, run cooler, and breathe deeper.
Yes, the unexpected will still strike at the worst possible time. But it will no longer ruin the moment, let alone your whole day. A penny on the tracks, nothing more.
